## 2. Impact

This section addresses the Impact criterion (evaluation weight: 30%) of the application to call HORIZON-MSCA-2026-PF-01-01 (MSCA Postdoctoral Fellowships 2026). It covers the career perspectives and employability of Dr. Rositsa Cholakova (sub-section 2.1); the dissemination, exploitation, and communication strategy (sub-section 2.2); and the scientific, societal, economic, and environmental impact (sub-section 2.3). Together the three sub-sections address all seven call-level expected impacts (EI-01 through EI-07) specified in HORIZON-MSCA-2026-PF-01-01 through project-specific mechanisms grounded in the five-work-package structure: Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state (WP1), Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration (WP2), Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration (WP3), Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge (WP4), and Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management (WP5).

### 2.1 Career perspectives and employability of the researcher

#### 2.1.1 The fellowship's career development rationale

Dr. Rositsa Cholakova enters the fellowship at approximately four years post-PhD, having completed her doctoral work summa cum laude in 2020 on the non-destructive evaluation of the physiological status of drought-stressed tomato plants (doi:10.2139/ssrn.5492527), with further peer-reviewed contributions on maize chilling-stress photosynthesis and biostimulants. Her research line is internally coherent: plant physiology, non-destructive evaluation of abiotic and biotic plant stress, and crop monitoring, centred at the Maritsa Vegetable Crops Research Institute, Bulgarian Agricultural Academy, Plovdiv, Bulgaria.

This expertise is the fellowship's principal justification from the fellow-to-host direction of the two-way knowledge transfer. Dr. Cholakova supplies the biological ground-truth engine — non-destructive physiological measurement of chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy and leaf temperature, and spectral reflectance (RQ4) — without which the field validation work of WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration) would be methodologically ungrounded. The Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics geoinformatics group at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest cannot supply this expertise internally. Route B's covarying-patch design (RQ2) rests on a plant-physiological hypothesis — that a nearby homogeneous semi-natural patch covaries biologically with the target tomato crop — whose operationalisation and experimental proof (co-located seasonal campaign, RQ9) require the measurement toolkit and physiological interpretation that constitute the fellow's doctoral expertise.

The host-to-fellow direction is equally substantive. Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics provides geoinformatics and remote-sensing infrastructure, the hyperspectral imaging, field spectroscopy, and multisensor-drone fusion methods at the core of WP1, and the computational and Earth-observation framework within which the fellow's physiological insights are transformed into probabilistic, satellite-informed field-state estimates and irrigation decisions. Supervisor Dr. András Jung — Deputy Head of the Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics, Head of the Multisensor-Drone-Fusion Working Group (project ELTE TKP2021-NVA-29), co-founder of Cubert GmbH and Brightic Research, habilitations in Computer Science and Crop Sciences — anchors this transfer. His dual habilitation signals that the disciplinary bridge this fellowship crosses has been independently traversed and is intellectually navigable.

The fellowship advances Dr. Rositsa Cholakova from postdoctoral researcher toward a cross-disciplinary profile at the intersection of plant physiology and non-destructive stress phenotyping with geoinformatics, probabilistic remote sensing, and uncertainty-aware crop modelling. This profile opens career paths in academic research groups specialising in remote sensing, crop science, or precision agriculture; in the agri-tech sector; and in research management roles requiring methodological breadth across environmental sensing and decision support. The project's confirmed TRL target — research prototype, TRL 3-4 (RQ10) — is proportionate to a 24-month European Fellowship: it delivers a research prototype and its foundational scientific evidence, not a commercial product. The mobility from Plovdiv, Bulgaria to ELTE, Budapest, Hungary (intra-EU) satisfies the MSCA-PF mobility requirement and constitutes a European Fellowship (EF, 24 months).

#### 2.1.2 Career Development Plan

The formal governance instrument for the fellow's career development is the Career Development Plan (D4-01, WP4: Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge), prepared jointly by Dr. András Jung and Dr. Rositsa Cholakova and submitted as a project deliverable at the beginning of the action (month 3), in line with scope requirement SR-04 of HORIZON-MSCA-2026-PF-01-01. The Career Development Plan is reviewed and updated during the fellowship, providing auditable evidence of two-way knowledge transfer progression and training plan execution. It covers research objectives, the fellow's training and career needs across all mandatory transferable-skills dimensions, publication plans, and open science activities.

D4-01 is the operative instrument through which this fellowship realises EI-01 (improved employability and career prospects), EI-05 (alignment with the European Charter for Researchers via jointly prepared, periodically reviewed, transparent supervision arrangements), EI-07 (new mind-sets fostered through the formally documented interdisciplinary exchange), and EI-02 (enhanced networking and communication capacities as a named training goal). Specific quantitative career targets — publication counts, training hours, thesis co-supervision, follow-on proposal timing — are to be set jointly by Dr. András Jung and Dr. Rositsa Cholakova in the Career Development Plan at action start and tracked through its review cycle. These targets are the CDP's content, not the proposal's content; they depend on the fellow's evolving research outputs and the supervisor's mentorship capacity and cannot be fixed externally to the supervisory relationship.

#### 2.1.3 Structured training in the MSCA-PF mandatory dimensions

The fellowship's training programme integrates all key transferable skills and competences required by scope requirement SR-03 (HORIZON-MSCA-2026-PF-01-01):

**Digital and AI skills, including the responsible use of generative AI in remote-sensing and crop-water modelling and scientific coding.** The project's methodological core — probabilistic machine learning for multi-sensor Earth observation crop-water-state estimation — is the training environment. Dr. Cholakova develops competences in probabilistic inference, Bayesian calibration, uncertainty quantification, and model validation through WP1 and WP2 research tasks. The responsible use of generative AI is addressed in the disciplinary contexts where it matters for this project: remote-sensing analysis pipelines, crop-water modelling, and scientific coding, where uncritical automation risks producing calibration errors that would undermine the honest-uncertainty commitment.

**Knowledge valorisation, innovation and entrepreneurship.** The project translates the uncertainty-aware demonstrator (D2-01, WP2) toward user uptake, with associated partner AgroVIR providing the farmer-interface feedback channel. Dr. András Jung, as co-founder of Cubert GmbH and Brightic Research, provides mentorship in knowledge valorisation grounded in a demonstrated personal track record of translating research instrumentation from laboratory to commercial deployment.

**Research integrity and open science ethics, including FAIR data stewardship.** The project commits to open-access publication, FAIR release of all primary data and software, and an open validation protocol enabling independent replication. The Data Management Plan (D5-01, WP5: Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management), delivered by month 6, operationalises FAIR compliance across WP1 through WP3 data assets. Research integrity is embedded at the methodological level: the 90% prediction-interval coverage criterion (RQ5) is the project's adopted definition of honest uncertainty, ensuring that research integrity in the scientific-conduct sense is inseparable from the methods being learned.

#### 2.1.4 Two-way transfer of knowledge

The two-way knowledge transfer is the defining structural mechanism of this fellowship.

The fellow-to-host direction is substantive and non-substitutable: Dr. Cholakova's non-destructive stress-phenotyping expertise (chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy and leaf temperature, spectral reflectance, RQ4) is the ground-truth methodology for WP3 and the biological design logic behind Route B (RQ2). ELTE's geoinformatics group cannot supply this expertise internally. The host-to-fellow direction is equally substantive: Dr. Jung's group provides geoinformatics and remote-sensing infrastructure, hyperspectral and multisensor-drone fusion methods (Multisensor-Drone-Fusion Working Group, ELTE TKP2021-NVA-29), and the computational framework within which physiological observations are transformed into probabilistic field-state estimates and irrigation decisions. The exchange is formally structured in WP4 (Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge) and documented in D4-01 (Career Development Plan).

The inter-sectoral dimension is provided by associated partner AgroVIR (Hungary) — a non-academic actor in the Hungarian agricultural sector whose involvement in WP3 field validation and D2-01 demonstrator feedback creates genuine research-to-practice boundary-crossing. AgroVIR provides farmer access and field-validation site logistics; it does not own or operate any project output.

This two-way transfer directly realises EI-07 (new mind-sets through international, inter-sectoral and interdisciplinary experience), EI-03 (stronger R&I capacity and knowledge transfer among participating organisations), and EI-02 (enhanced networking and communication capacities, through WP4 training in scientific communication).

#### 2.1.5 Contribution to EI-01

The jointly prepared Career Development Plan (D4-01, month 3) covering all mandatory training dimensions, genuine two-way knowledge transfer producing a cross-disciplinary profile in plant physiology and probabilistic geoinformatics, and the research portfolio from WP1-WP3 (outcomes OUT-1, OUT-2, OUT-3, OUT-4) together constitute the fellowship's contribution to EI-01: improved employability and career prospects of MSCA postdoctoral fellows within academia and beyond, contributing to a more mobile and highly skilled European research workforce.

### 2.2 Dissemination, exploitation and communication

#### 2.2.1 Governance: Data Management Plan and Dissemination and exploitation plan

Two deliverables under WP5 (Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management) establish the formal governance for all dissemination and exploitation activity, both due at month 6 — before any primary research deliverable is complete — ensuring open-access routes and FAIR compliance are confirmed in advance of the outputs they govern.

The Data Management Plan (D5-01, WP5: Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management), due month 6, defines the FAIR-principles compliance framework for all primary research data generated in WP1, WP2, and WP3, governing findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability for multi-sensor EO datasets, probabilistic model code, and the Hungarian tomato field validation dataset.

The Dissemination and exploitation plan (D5-02, WP5: Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management), due month 6, identifies open-access dissemination routes for all three work packages' primary outputs and establishes the timeline and channels for scientific communication and public engagement. D5-02 is the operative instrument for EI-04 (increased attractiveness, visibility, and reputation of Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest and the ERA) through internationally positioned dissemination addressing an identified literature gap.

#### 2.2.2 Scientific dissemination: publications and open-source outputs

The primary scientific dissemination outputs are the peer-reviewed open-access publications arising from WP1-WP3, constituting project outcome OUT-5 (Peer-reviewed publications and open science outputs, WP5). Publications cover the probabilistic multi-sensor field-state diagnosis method (OUT-1, WP1), the uncertainty-aware AquaCrop decision engine (OUT-2, WP2), and the field-validation dataset and uncertainty-calibration evidence (OUT-3, WP3). All publications are made available under open-access routes in compliance with the Horizon Europe open-access mandate and D5-01, confirmed by D5-02 at month 6. Target audiences include the geoinformatics, remote sensing, and precision agriculture research communities positioned to evaluate the project's specific novelty: the end-to-end probabilistic coupling of multi-sensor Earth observation, crop-water-state estimation (root-zone soil moisture and crop water status, RQ3), and WUE-oriented irrigation decision support (RQ6).

The open-source release of project software constitutes a second durable dissemination channel. The probabilistic diagnosis code accompanying the Diagnostic model specification and calibration report (D1-01, month 14) is released as an open-source repository under FAIR principles (confirmed by D5-01). The Decision engine and demonstrator software (D2-01, month 20) is released as an open-source artefact providing the global precision agriculture and crop-modelling community with a reproducible, openly licensed implementation of the full end-to-end pipeline from Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical, and PlanetScope (RQ8) observations through probabilistic crop-water-state diagnosis through uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration and counterfactual simulation to WUE-optimised irrigation recommendation (RQ6). The Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report (D3-01, month 24) is released under a dataset DOI or open repository reference under FAIR principles, providing an internationally reproducible benchmark from Hungarian tomato field sites for the probabilistic diagnosis framework and Route B covariation validation (RQ9).

#### 2.2.3 Communication to non-specialist audiences

Associated partner AgroVIR (Hungary) is the primary channel for communicating results to non-specialist audiences — Hungarian tomato farmers and the horticultural sector. AgroVIR's farmer access and field-validation logistics for WP3 create the operational agricultural context in which D2-01's decision-support outputs are presented to and critiqued by real agricultural users. This is an integral part of the project's scientific validation pathway: operational agricultural feedback directly informs the assessment of the demonstrator's usability at TRL 3-4 and tests the real-world credibility of WUE-optimised irrigation recommendations.

Curriculum integration at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest constitutes a second communication channel, reaching MSc and PhD students in geoinformatics, remote sensing, and precision agriculture programmes. D1-01 and D2-01, released as open-source code under D5-01, provide concrete teachable advances in Bayesian multi-sensor fusion and uncertainty-aware crop-water decision support integrable into ELTE's academic teaching — realising EI-06 (regular feedback of research results into teaching and education at participating organisations).

#### 2.2.4 Exploitation strategy and intellectual property

All primary research outputs — D1-01 (Diagnostic model specification and calibration report), D2-01 (Decision engine and demonstrator software), and D3-01 (Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report) — are research artefacts intended for open dissemination. No patent protection is sought. The project operates at TRL 3-4 (RQ10), and the primary value of its outputs is their contribution to the scientific literature and open-source knowledge base. The Decision engine and demonstrator software (D2-01) is the key exploitation vehicle: a replicable, openly licensed end-to-end decision-support prototype available to the global precision agriculture research community for further development and future TRL progression. Post-fellowship sustainability is secured through the open-infrastructure pathway: Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest retains the validated methodology, code (D1-01, D2-01), and benchmark dataset (D3-01) as open research infrastructure within its Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics, enabling continued use and extension beyond the fellowship period.

#### 2.2.5 Contribution to EI-02

Peer-reviewed open-access publications (OUT-5, WP5), FAIR data and software release (D1-01, D2-01, D3-01 confirmed by D5-01 and D5-02 at month 6), AgroVIR-mediated communication to the agricultural sector (WP3), and curriculum integration at ELTE — all embedded in WP5 and governed by mandatory deliverables — constitute the project's contribution to EI-02: increased and broadened research and innovation impact through enhanced networking and communication capacities with scientific peers and the general public. The fellow is trained in scientific communication and networking through WP4 (documented in D4-01), providing the communication competence to disseminate WP1-WP3 substantive outputs effectively.

### 2.3 Scientific, societal and economic impact

#### 2.3.1 Overview

The project generates impact through four complementary pathways, all calibrated to the confirmed TRL 3-4 research prototype target (RQ10): IMP-1 (Scientific advance in probabilistic multi-sensor crop-water-state estimation), IMP-2 (Economic and societal impact: water-use efficiency and farm resilience), IMP-3 (Environmental co-benefit through landscape-compatible sensing), and IMP-4 (Advancement of the researcher's career and the European Research Area, addressed primarily in sub-section 2.1). No claim asserts operational deployment, commercial uptake, scaled water savings, or quantified agricultural economic benefits that would be premature for a 24-month, single-researcher European Fellowship producing a research prototype.

#### 2.3.2 IMP-1: Scientific advance in probabilistic multi-sensor crop-water-state estimation

The project's primary scientific contribution is establishing a defensible end-to-end probabilistic framework in a specific, documented literature gap. The gap is stated precisely: across the reviewed studies, occurrence counts fall steeply as sensor integration deepens and as the task shifts from monitoring toward real-time decision support; the intersection of real-time decision support with PlanetScope high-resolution imagery is the single empty cell of the systematic literature review's research-gap matrix. This is a reviewable, specific, and narrow claim grounded in a review of 50 studies.

WP1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state) develops and calibrates Route B — the homogeneous-patch proxy (RQ2) — fusing Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical, secured PlanetScope imagery (RQ8), ERA5 meteorological reanalysis, and field observations into posterior estimates of root-zone soil moisture and crop water status (RQ3) for tomato (RQ1) at Hungarian field sites via AgroVIR. The Diagnostic model specification and calibration report (D1-01, month 14) is the primary scientific deliverable. Route A (direct probabilistic fusion) is also defined in the project architecture as a rigorous one-step alternative sharing the same downstream decision engine, maintaining the methodological breadth needed for a credible literature contribution.

WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration) calibrates AquaCrop while retaining an honest parameter posterior, runs counterfactual irrigation simulations over weather ensembles, and recommends the option that best improves WUE (RQ6). The Decision engine and demonstrator software (D2-01, month 20) delivers the end-to-end coupling from multi-sensor observation through probabilistic crop-water-state estimation to uncertainty-aware irrigation decision recommendation — the integration the literature gap identifies as underdeveloped.

WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration) tests the framework against non-destructive physiological ground truth (chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy and leaf temperature, spectral reflectance, RQ4) and validates uncertainty calibration using the 90% prediction-interval coverage criterion (RQ5) — the project's adopted definition of honest uncertainty and pilot-success criterion (RQ7). The Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report (D3-01, month 24) constitutes this evidence together with the co-located seasonal campaign demonstrating statistical covariation between the proxy patch and the target tomato crop (RQ9).

The novelty argument is defended against the identified precedents — Bayesian Maximum Entropy drought fusion, copula-based drought-irrigation scheduling, dynamic Bayesian networks, MF-FusionNet — by the specific combination that each precedent lacks: all three of learned multimodal fusion, explicit probabilistic crop-water-state estimation, and WUE-oriented decision optimisation propagating uncertainty end-to-end. The precedents are respected, not dismissed. This scientific advance produces outcomes OUT-1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor field-state diagnosis method), OUT-2 (Uncertainty-aware AquaCrop decision engine), OUT-3 (Field-validation dataset and uncertainty-calibration evidence), and OUT-5 (Peer-reviewed publications and open science outputs), and directly contributes to EI-03 (stronger R&I capacity at ELTE), EI-04 (increased visibility of ELTE and the ERA), and EI-06 (research results feeding into ELTE teaching).

#### 2.3.3 IMP-2: Economic and societal impact: water-use efficiency and farm resilience

The project's confirmed decision objective is water-use efficiency (WUE, RQ6), chosen explicitly over yield maximisation or profit maximisation. The framework scores candidate irrigation decisions by WUE under the uncertainty propagated from WP1 diagnosis and the WP2 weather ensemble, recommending the option with the best expected WUE. The economic and societal relevance is direct: over-irrigation imposes direct economic costs (water, energy) and indirect environmental and social costs (runoff, soil degradation, shared water-resource pressure). An uncertainty-aware framework calibrating irrigation to actual crop-water status from multi-sensor Earth observation, rather than from generic scheduling tables, addresses over-irrigation at its methodological source.

The impact pathway is: WP1 (root-zone soil moisture and crop water status diagnosis) to WP2 (WUE-optimised counterfactual simulation) to D2-01 (Decision engine and demonstrator software) to outcomes OUT-2 (Uncertainty-aware AquaCrop decision engine) and OUT-4 (Standalone research demonstrator (web MVP)) to farmers and agri-tech stakeholders reached through AgroVIR. The pilot-success criterion (RQ7) — the 90% prediction-interval coverage target (RQ5) met on the validation set — is the project's verifiable threshold for whether the diagnostic and decision framework is credible enough to underpin its economic impact claim. Impact magnitudes are not asserted beyond TRL 3-4: the project establishes the probabilistic scientific basis for WUE-optimised irrigation recommendation for tomato horticulture, validated at Hungarian field sites, providing the foundation on which future higher-TRL development would build.

#### 2.3.4 IMP-3: Environmental co-benefit through landscape-compatible sensing

Route B (RQ2) sidesteps the sub-pixel resolution problem by selecting a nearby, homogeneous, semi-natural covarying patch that the coarse satellite pixel can resolve cleanly. This aligns the sensing methodology with landscape sustainability in a structurally significant way: the sensing strategy is positively correlated with the presence of natural or semi-natural patches in the agricultural landscape. A farmer who retains a semi-natural patch at the field margin gains a better-performing observation proxy; a landscape from which such patches are eliminated loses the observational infrastructure on which Route B depends. This co-benefit is a structural property of the methodology, not post-hoc framing.

The co-benefit is operationalised through WP3 via the co-located seasonal campaign testing the patch-covariation assumption (RQ9). The Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report (D3-01, month 24) and its embedded Route B covariation evidence document this result. The environmental co-benefit is stated as a structural upside of the confirmed methodology, not as a quantified environmental gain beyond the project's TRL 3-4 scope.

#### 2.3.5 IMP-4: ERA capacity and the host institution

Beyond Dr. Rositsa Cholakova's career contribution (sub-section 2.1), the project strengthens Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest in two ways. First, WP1-WP3 produce genuine additions to ELTE's research output — D1-01 (Diagnostic model specification and calibration report), D2-01 (Decision engine and demonstrator software), D3-01 (Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report) — in remote sensing, probabilistic machine learning, and precision agriculture decision support, extending the Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics research capacity into crop-water-state diagnostics and strengthening ELTE's R&I output (EI-03). Second, open publication and FAIR release of results addressing the identified literature gap increase ELTE's international citation footprint and reputation in multi-sensor EO and uncertainty-quantification communities, enhancing ELTE's attractiveness as a fellowship host and research partner (EI-04). The project's hosting at ELTE in Budapest, Hungary — a Horizon Europe widening country — situates this contribution within the ERA's objective of balanced scientific excellence across Member States.

#### 2.3.6 Summary: call expected impacts mapped to project mechanisms

EI-01: realised through WP4 (D4-01, Career Development Plan, month 3) via two-way knowledge transfer and mandatory training programme.

EI-02: realised through WP5 (D5-01, Data Management Plan, month 6; D5-02, Dissemination and exploitation plan, month 6) via open-access publications (OUT-5), FAIR data and software release (D1-01, D2-01, D3-01), and communication training in D4-01.

EI-03: realised through WP1 (D1-01), WP2 (D2-01), and WP4 (D4-01), strengthening ELTE's research output and enacting bi-directional disciplinary exchange between Dr. Cholakova's plant-physiology expertise and Dr. Jung's geoinformatics group.

EI-04: realised through D5-02 (Dissemination and exploitation plan, month 6) and D3-01 (Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report, month 24) released as FAIR benchmarks addressing the identified literature gap, increasing ELTE's international profile.

EI-05: realised through D4-01 (Career Development Plan, month 3) implementing charter-aligned supervision, regular career reviews, and equitable mandatory training coverage.

EI-06: realised through WP1 (D1-01) and WP5 (D5-01, Data Management Plan, month 6) producing open-source code and FAIR data assets integrable into ELTE's geoinformatics and remote-sensing curricula.

EI-07: realised through the Bulgaria-to-Hungary intra-EU mobility, the plant-physiology-to-geoinformatics interdisciplinary exchange documented in WP4 (D4-01) and WP1 (D1-01), and AgroVIR's inter-sectoral engagement in WP3.

### 2.1 Credibility of the measures to enhance the career perspectives and employability of the researcher and contribution to his/her skills development

#### 2.1.1 Point of departure: Dr. Rositsa Cholakova's career position and the development logic of the fellowship

Dr. Rositsa Cholakova enters this European Fellowship approximately four years post-PhD, having completed her doctoral work summa cum laude in 2020 on the non-destructive evaluation of the physiological status of drought-stressed tomato plants (doi:10.2139/ssrn.5492527), with additional peer-reviewed contributions on maize chilling-stress photosynthesis and biostimulants. Her position at the Maritsa Vegetable Crops Research Institute, Bulgarian Agricultural Academy, Plovdiv, Bulgaria establishes her at the productive core of an agroecological research ecosystem in which plant physiology, non-destructive measurement, and crop stress monitoring are the primary scientific activities.

The fellowship is designed not to replicate this competence profile within a different host institution but to expand it into a substantially different disciplinary space: geoinformatics, probabilistic remote sensing, and uncertainty-aware crop-water decision-support modelling. This disciplinary expansion is the fellowship's career development logic. The mechanism through which it operates is a genuine bilateral capability exchange — not a hosting arrangement in which the fellow consumes training provided by the host, but a structured scientific partnership in which each party contributes capabilities the other cannot generate internally.

Dr. Cholakova's contribution to the exchange is the biological ground-truth engine that makes the project's validation methodology credible. The non-destructive physiological measurement of chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy and leaf temperature, and spectral reflectance (RQ4) is the scientific toolkit with which she collects the plant-physiological ground truth in WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration), against which the probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis framework is calibrated. Without this expertise, Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest's Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics cannot conduct the WP3 validation protocol independently: the geoinformatics and remote-sensing group's competences are complementary to, not overlapping with, the fellow's plant-physiological measurement skills. This non-substitutability is the structural basis for the bilateral transfer claim and it makes the career development impact of the fellowship credible rather than nominal, resting on a real and verifiable disciplinary dependency.

Dr. Cholakova's doctoral thesis — on the non-destructive evaluation of drought-stressed tomato plants, the exact species (RQ1) and water-deficit stress type central to this project's field validation — means the transferred expertise is domain-specific and immediately productive for the host's research programme, not general and peripheral. The mutual dependency runs in both directions: just as the host requires the fellow's phenotyping competence, the fellow requires the host's geoinformatics infrastructure and probabilistic remote-sensing methods to execute WP1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state) and WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration).

The fellowship's intra-EU mobility — from Plovdiv, Bulgaria to ELTE, Budapest, Hungary — constitutes this action as a European Fellowship (EF, 24 months) meeting the MSCA mobility requirement (SR-01), and converts that mobility into career capital by embedding it within a scientific collaboration structured around a genuine capability gap on both sides.

#### 2.1.2 The Career Development Plan: governance, content, and accountability cycle

The primary formal governance instrument for the fellow's career development is the Career Development Plan (D4-01, WP4: Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge), prepared jointly by Dr. András Jung and Dr. Rositsa Cholakova and submitted as a project deliverable at the beginning of the action (month 3), in accordance with scope requirement SR-04 of HORIZON-MSCA-2026-PF-01-01. This deliverable date — month 3 — is confirmed in the canonical reference pack and places the CDP submission before any primary research deliverable, ensuring that the supervision framework and training plan are established at action start rather than retrospectively.

The Career Development Plan operationalises the fellowship's career development commitments in four interlocking respects. First, it establishes the research objectives jointly — the supervisor's assessment of feasibility and scientific ambition is integrated with the fellow's research aims from the outset, not imposed after the fact. Second, it records the fellow's training and career needs across all mandatory transferable-skills dimensions specified by SR-03 — a structured, externally reviewed training plan that makes the development trajectory explicit and auditable. Third, it covers publication plans and open science activities, anchoring the fellow's scientific output commitments and her FAIR-compliance obligations (operationalised in the Data Management Plan, D5-01, WP5: Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management, month 6) within the CDP governance cycle. Fourth, and critically for credibility, the Career Development Plan is reviewed and updated during the fellowship — creating the periodic reassessment mechanism that keeps it a live supervisory instrument rather than a month-3 artefact filed and forgotten.

The joint authorship of the Career Development Plan by Dr. András Jung is substantively credible, not merely procedurally compliant. Dr. Jung holds habilitations in both Computer Science and Crop Sciences, serves as Deputy Head of the Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics, and is Head of the Multisensor-Drone-Fusion Working Group (ELTE TKP2021-NVA-29). As co-founder of Cubert GmbH and Brightic Research, he has demonstrated direct personal experience of translating research instrumentation from laboratory to commercial deployment — the knowledge valorisation pathway that constitutes one of the fellowship's mandatory training dimensions. His habilitations in two disciplines that span the exact bridge this fellowship crosses — computational science and crop science — mean that his co-authorship of D4-01 provides the fellow with supervisory guidance from someone who has independently traversed the disciplinary boundary from biological crop science toward computational remote sensing and has a verifiable track record on both sides. This supervisor profile is not a procedural credential but a substantive career development resource.

The Career Development Plan is the operative instrument through which this fellowship realises EI-01 (improved employability and career prospects of MSCA postdoctoral fellows within academia and beyond, contributing to a more mobile and highly skilled European research workforce) and EI-05 (increased alignment of working conditions for researchers in accordance with the principles set out in the European Charter for Researchers), and contributes to EO-04 (increased alignment of working conditions in accordance with the Charter) and EO-05 (enhanced quality and sustainability of research training and supervision). Charter alignment is delivered through jointly prepared, periodically reviewed, transparent supervision arrangements in which the fellow's career needs are documented, reviewed, and held accountable by both parties under a contractually binding deliverable framework. No specific quantitative career targets — publication counts, training hours, thesis co-supervision arrangements — are fixed in this proposal. These are the Career Development Plan's substance, established by the supervisor-fellow partnership at action start in light of the actual research workload and evolving outputs; prescribing them externally in advance would undermine rather than support the charter-aligned supervision principle that D4-01 is designed to realise.

#### 2.1.3 Scientific and technical competence acquisition through WP1–WP3 research

The most durable career development measure in this fellowship is the acquisition of new, demonstrable scientific and technical competences through the research work itself. The competences acquired through WP1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state), WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration), and WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration) are the basis for publication, for independent grant applications, and for the cross-disciplinary career profile that the fellowship aims to produce. Because these competences are acquired by doing the research — not by attending courses about it — their acquisition is verifiable through the research outputs they generate: D1-01 (Diagnostic model specification and calibration report, month 14), D2-01 (Decision engine and demonstrator software, month 20), and D3-01 (Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report, month 24).

**WP1: Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state.** This work package requires Dr. Cholakova to develop proficiency in: harmonising heterogeneous Earth observation datasets including Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical, and secured PlanetScope imagery (RQ8), together with ERA5 meteorological reanalysis; specifying and calibrating a probabilistic model that returns posterior estimates of the latent field state (root-zone soil moisture and crop water status, RQ3) as a full probability distribution rather than a point estimate; and implementing Route B — the homogeneous-patch proxy (RQ2) — within a methodological architecture that also defines Route A (direct probabilistic fusion) as a rigorous alternative. Working under Dr. Jung's direct supervision within the Multisensor-Drone-Fusion Working Group, Dr. Cholakova gains access to the group's hyperspectral imaging, field spectroscopy, and multisensor-drone fusion methodology and infrastructure — competences specific to this supervision context and not generally available through standard academic training programmes. The primary deliverable, the Diagnostic model specification and calibration report (D1-01, WP1), is a peer-reviewable scientific document that constitutes the public, citable evidence of this competence acquisition.

**WP2: Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration.** The prognostic decision-engine work requires competences in: uncertainty-aware calibration of the FAO AquaCrop crop model retaining an honest parameter posterior; counterfactual irrigation simulation over weather ensembles; water-use-efficiency-based decision recommendation under uncertainty (RQ6); and integration of the diagnostic and prognostic modules into a standalone research demonstrator. The specific combination of Bayesian crop-model calibration with weather-ensemble scenario evaluation and WUE-optimised recommendation is the technical competence that positions Dr. Cholakova to design and conduct uncertainty-aware agri-environmental decision-support research independently after the fellowship — across crop species and geographies beyond the tomato horticulture context of this project. The Decision engine and demonstrator software (D2-01, WP2, month 20) constitutes the software artefact evidencing this competence.

**WP3: Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration.** The validation work package is the site where the fellow's existing plant-physiology competences are operationalised within a new scientific context. She leads the collection of non-destructive physiological ground truth (RQ4: chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy and leaf temperature, spectral reflectance) — the measurement domain where her doctoral expertise is directly load-bearing — while simultaneously acquiring competence in probabilistic validation methodology: prediction-interval coverage assessment (RQ5: 90% prediction intervals containing the truth approximately 90% of the time), pilot-success evaluation (RQ7: the RQ5 calibration target met on the validation set), and Route B covariation testing via a co-located seasonal campaign measuring the proxy patch and target tomato crop simultaneously (RQ9). WP3 is the work package in which the fellow most visibly operates as both knowledge provider (plant-physiological measurement) and knowledge acquirer (probabilistic calibration and covariation testing methodology), making it the most intensive site of genuine bilateral competence exchange in the project. The Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report (D3-01, WP3, month 24) is the archival validation artefact evidencing this work.

Taken together, the WP1–WP3 research outputs — D1-01, D2-01, and D3-01 — constitute a publicly available, FAIR-released portfolio of original scientific contributions that serve as the empirical evidence base for Dr. Cholakova's post-fellowship career applications across academic research, the non-academic agri-tech sector, and research management. These deliverables are not career development intentions; they are contractual deliverables with confirmed due months and confirmed content specifications.

#### 2.1.4 Structured transferable-skills training in the MSCA-PF mandatory dimensions

The fellowship's training programme integrates all key transferable skills and competences required by scope requirement SR-03 of HORIZON-MSCA-2026-PF-01-01, covering digital skills (including generative AI), Open Science, knowledge valorisation, innovation and entrepreneurship, and research integrity. The training is embedded in the project's own research activities and the host institution's research environment, ensuring that competence acquisition is contextualised within the domain of application rather than delivered as generic external modules:

**Digital and AI skills, including the responsible use of generative AI in remote-sensing and crop-water modelling and scientific coding.** The project's core methodology — probabilistic machine learning for multi-sensor Earth observation crop-water-state estimation and uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration — constitutes the digital and AI training environment. Dr. Cholakova acquires hands-on proficiency in probabilistic inference, Bayesian model calibration, uncertainty quantification, and computational model validation through the WP1 and WP2 research activities. The responsible use of generative AI is addressed in the specific disciplinary contexts where it carries methodological risk for this project: remote-sensing analysis pipelines, crop-water modelling, and scientific coding, where uncritical automation can introduce calibration artefacts that would undermine the honest-uncertainty commitment operationalised by RQ5. This domain-specific treatment of generative AI responsibility — integrating it into the technical methodology rather than as a standalone ethics module — provides training that is immediately applicable and is grounded in the concrete failure modes that matter for probabilistic Earth observation crop-water modelling.

**Knowledge valorisation, innovation and entrepreneurship.** Mentorship in knowledge valorisation is provided by Dr. András Jung, whose co-founding of Cubert GmbH and Brightic Research demonstrates a personal track record of translating research instrumentation from laboratory to commercial deployment. This is not entrepreneurship pedagogy but applied experiential mentorship from a supervisor with documented first-hand experience of the relevant translation path. The project's demonstrator-based approach — producing the Decision engine and demonstrator software (D2-01, WP2) as an open-source research artefact designed for user uptake — provides the practical context within which knowledge valorisation training operates. AgroVIR, the associated partner, provides the farmer-interface feedback channel through which demonstrator uptake is tested against real agricultural users, closing the loop between research output and practice-facing assessment.

**Research integrity and open science ethics, including FAIR data stewardship.** The fellowship's open-science posture is operationalised through the Data Management Plan (D5-01, WP5: Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management, month 6), which defines the FAIR-principles compliance framework for all primary research data generated in WP1–WP3 before those data are collected — a forward-looking governance commitment rather than a retrospective compliance audit. Research integrity is embedded at the methodological level through RQ5: the 90% prediction-interval coverage criterion is both the project's technical calibration standard and its definition of honest scientific reporting. A model that reports what it does not know with the same rigour as what it knows is simultaneously applying a technical methodology and implementing a research-conduct principle. The project treats these as structurally equivalent rather than as separate domains, providing the fellow with an integrated understanding of research integrity that arises from doing the research rather than from attending compliance training.

All three transferable-skills dimensions are directly grounded in the project's specific research content, the supervisor's specific professional background, and named deliverables that provide evidence of training completion and governance (D4-01 as the CDP recording the training plan; D5-01 as the FAIR governance commitment). This grounding is the basis for the claimed credibility of the training measures: they are embedded in the scientific activities the fellow will actually perform and cannot be decoupled from the research without the research itself collapsing.

#### 2.1.5 Two-way knowledge transfer, international mobility, and inter-sectoral exposure

The two-way transfer of knowledge operationalised through WP4 (Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge) and documented in D4-01 (Career Development Plan, month 3) is the structural mechanism that distinguishes this fellowship as an MSCA career development action rather than a standard postdoctoral appointment.

**Fellow-to-host transfer (plant physiology to geoinformatics).** Dr. Cholakova's non-destructive stress-phenotyping expertise — chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy and leaf temperature, spectral reflectance (RQ4) — is the plant-physiological measurement layer that makes WP3 methodologically credible. Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest's Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics cannot provide this expertise from within its existing personnel. The transfer is therefore genuinely bilateral: the fellow brings into the host's geoinformatics research group a biological measurement capability that does not exist there, permanently expanding the group's capacity for plant-physiology-grounded validation of crop-water-state remote sensing beyond the duration of the fellowship. The permanence of this contribution — the validation methodology and the ground-truth dataset (D3-01) remain at ELTE as open research infrastructure — is the basis for the claim that this is a knowledge transfer, not merely a visiting appointment.

**Host-to-fellow transfer (geoinformatics to plant physiology).** Dr. Jung's Multisensor-Drone-Fusion Working Group (ELTE TKP2021-NVA-29) provides the geoinformatics and remote-sensing infrastructure, hyperspectral imaging and field spectroscopy methods, and the computational Earth observation framework within which the fellow's plant-physiological insights are transformed into probabilistic, satellite-informed field-state estimates and irrigation decision recommendations. The competence transfer is concrete and measurable: Dr. Cholakova's ability after the fellowship to design and execute a probabilistic multi-sensor fusion pipeline from Earth observation to field-state diagnosis (WP1) and to calibrate an uncertainty-aware crop model for WUE-optimised decision recommendation (WP2) are competences that exist at the host before the fellowship and are not currently in the fellow's profile. Their transfer is evidenced by the research outputs that could only have been produced through active engagement with those methods.

**International mobility between Bulgaria and Hungary.** The intra-EU move from Plovdiv, Bulgaria to Budapest, Hungary exposes the fellow to a different national research environment, institutional culture, research group organisation, and country-level science policy context within the European Research Area. This international experience is a career asset in both academic and non-academic hiring and contributes directly to the MSCA programme objective of producing a more mobile and highly skilled European research workforce. The fellowship's hosting at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest — in Hungary — additionally situates the ERA capacity contribution within the ERA's objective of balanced scientific excellence across Member States.

**Inter-sectoral exposure through AgroVIR.** AgroVIR (Hungary), as a non-academic associated partner operating in the Hungarian agricultural sector, provides the fellowship's inter-sectoral boundary crossing. The fellow's interaction with AgroVIR in the context of WP3 field validation — encountering agricultural sector knowledge requirements, farmer decision-making contexts, and the user-uptake challenges of moving from research prototype (TRL 3-4, RQ10) to practical farm decision support — constitutes an employment-relevant competence for career paths in the agri-tech sector and in roles requiring translation between research and agricultural practice. AgroVIR provides farmer access and field-validation site logistics; it does not own or operate any project output. This inter-sectoral exposure contributes to EI-07 (new mind-sets and approaches to R&I work fostered through international, inter-sectoral and interdisciplinary experience) and is formally structured within WP4 and documented in D4-01.

The two-way transfer further realises EI-03 (stronger R&I capacity and output among participating organisations and better transfer of knowledge between participating organisations): Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest gains a permanent contribution to its research capacity in plant-physiology-grounded crop-water-state validation through the project's activities and open outputs, while the fellow carries the host's geoinformatics and remote-sensing competences into her subsequent research career.

#### 2.1.6 Contribution of the fellowship to the researcher's future career

The cross-disciplinary competence profile that the fellowship produces — a plant physiologist with demonstrated independent research capability in probabilistic multi-sensor Earth observation, uncertainty-aware crop-water modelling, and WUE-optimised decision support, evidenced by FAIR-released, peer-reviewable deliverables — is a specific and defensible career asset at the intersection of two active research communities (plant science and Earth observation) that individually generate large numbers of researchers but whose productive intersection remains underpopulated. This profile positions Dr. Rositsa Cholakova for career trajectories across multiple domains:

*Academic research.* Research groups in geoinformatics, remote sensing, crop science, and precision agriculture that pursue validated, uncertainty-quantified approaches to crop-water-state assessment require researchers who can bridge plant physiology and Earth observation. The fellow's demonstrated ability to produce a validated probabilistic framework — evidenced by the FAIR-released peer-reviewed outputs D1-01, D2-01, and D3-01 — provides an independently verifiable, citable record of technical capability. Open release of D1-01 (Diagnostic model specification and calibration report) and D2-01 (Decision engine and demonstrator software) as open-source research artefacts under D5-01's FAIR governance makes this record accessible to the international research community, supporting citation and collaboration opportunities that contribute to career visibility beyond ELTE.

*Non-academic and agri-tech sector.* The agri-tech sector and agricultural advisory services require researchers who can bridge raw Earth observation data and actionable farm decisions with quantified uncertainty. Dr. Cholakova's WP2 experience in the Uncertainty-aware AquaCrop decision engine (OUT-2: Uncertainty-aware AquaCrop decision engine) and her WP3 validation experience at real Hungarian tomato field sites through AgroVIR provide technically specific credentials for non-academic roles where demand for uncertainty-aware, physiologically grounded decision-support systems is growing but supply of researchers with demonstrated end-to-end implementation experience is limited.

*Research management and policy.* The successful execution of a 24-month, five-work-package MSCA-PF action — spanning WP1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state), WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration), WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration), WP4 (Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge), and WP5 (Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management) — under a European Fellowship governance framework develops project management, cross-disciplinary communication, open-science governance, and research-administration competences that are valued in research management and science policy roles.

This three-pathway career profile constitutes the fellowship's realisation of IMP-4 (Advancement of the researcher's career and the European Research Area), delivered through OBJ-5 (Advancement of the fellow's competences and career) and measurable through outcome OUT-6 (Enhanced researcher competences and career readiness) produced by WP4.

The cumulative contribution to EI-01 (improved employability and career prospects of MSCA postdoctoral fellows within academia and beyond, contributing to a more mobile and highly skilled European research workforce) is: the jointly prepared Career Development Plan (D4-01, month 3) establishing transparent, charter-aligned supervision with periodic review; scientific and technical competence acquisition through WP1–WP3 evidenced in peer-reviewed FAIR-released deliverables; mandatory transferable-skills training in all SR-03 dimensions embedded in the project's own research context and supervisor's documented professional background; genuine two-way knowledge transfer producing a cross-disciplinary profile not reproducible by either the fellow or the host acting alone; inter-sectoral exposure through AgroVIR creating agri-tech sector employment relevance; and intra-EU international mobility advancing the ERA's skilled and mobile research workforce objective. Each measure is grounded in a specific confirmed project activity, a named deliverable with a confirmed due month, or a confirmed supervisor characteristic — not in aspirational statements about career development disconnected from the project's scientific and structural content.
